What the official sources say

  • Landlord must itemize deductions in a written notice delivered to the tenant not more than 45 days after termination and delivery of possession; the landlord is not liable until the tenant supplies a written mailing address. (IC 32-31-3-12(a); source)
  • If a landlord fails to comply, the tenant may recover all of the deposit due and reasonable attorney's fees. (IC 32-31-3-12(b); source)
  • Landlord must mail an itemized damages list within 45 days after occupancy ends, with a refund check for the difference. (IC 32-31-3-14; source)
  • Landlord must deliver premises safe, clean and habitable, comply with health and housing codes, and maintain electrical, plumbing, sanitary, HVAC systems and supplied appliances. (IC 32-31-8-5; source)
  • A tenant may sue to enforce landlord obligations only after giving notice and a reasonable time to repair; prevailing tenant may recover damages, fees and injunctive relief. (IC 32-31-8-6; source)

Do Indiana cities set their own landlord and tenant rules?

Mostly no. Indiana Code 32-31-1-20 bars cities, towns and counties from regulating private rental housing unless a state statute authorizes it, so a landlord selling a rental in Fort Wayne works from the same statewide framework as one in Evansville.

The section names what a local government cannot control without state permission:

  • Rental rates, whether set through zoning or any other means.
  • Tenant screening and lease applications.
  • Security deposits and landlord fees.
  • Lease terms and conditions.
  • Required disclosures about the property, the lease or the parties' rights and duties.

Any local rule that crosses those lines is "void and unenforceable." There is one exception for privately owned housing that receives government funds or benefits to offer reduced rents to low or moderate income tenants. For an ordinary rental house, the state code in Title 32, Article 31 is the place to look first.

How much notice does it take to end a tenancy in Indiana?

The notice period depends on the type of tenancy and the reason. The lease can change the defaults, and the table shows what the statute sets when the lease is silent.

SituationNoticeStatute
Rent not paid when dueAt least 10 days, and the tenant can stop it by paying in full within the periodIC 32-31-1-6
Rental of three months or less that renews automaticallyNotice equal to one rental periodIC 32-31-1-4
Year-to-year tenancyAt least three months before the tenancy year endsIC 32-31-1-3
Landlord changes the rental agreementAt least 30 days in writing, unless a written agreement says otherwiseIC 32-31-5-4

Notice is a common stumbling block for sellers. A house advertised as vacant at closing usually needs a tenancy that has already ended in the way the statute and the lease require, so work backward from your target closing date and count the notice period before you set it.

What does an eviction case look like in Indiana?

An eviction is a court case, and the landlord cannot skip it. Indiana Legal Help describes a two-part process, with a possession hearing first and a damages hearing that often comes later.

  • Notice. For nonpayment or another lease violation, the landlord generally gives at least ten days notice. The tenant who pays in full or fixes the problem within that time cannot be removed on that notice.
  • Service. According to a fact sheet from Indiana Legal Services, the tenant receives a complaint, a notice of claim and a summons between 5 and 20 days before the court date, and the county sheriff usually delivers them.
  • Possession hearing. The court decides whether the tenant must move. In the common final outcome for nonpayment, the court sets a move-out date, typically two to three weeks away.
  • Immediate possession. A landlord can regain the unit soon after the hearing by paying money into court as a bond in case the eviction was wrong, and the tenant can pay the same amount to stay until the damages decision.
  • Damages hearing. The court can award back rent, utilities, property damage and fees to the landlord, or overpaid rent and repair costs to the tenant, within a $10,000 small claims limit.

After an eviction order, a motion to correct error or an appeal is due within 30 days. A tenant who misses the hearing and gets a default judgment may ask to vacate it for good cause within one year. Cases can be checked at mycase.in.gov.

Tenants in Indiana do not have the right to stop paying rent, which is a point sellers should keep in mind when a tenant raises repair complaints before a sale.

What may a landlord not do while preparing to sell?

A landlord may not lock out a tenant or cut off essential services, even when the goal is a vacant house for a quick sale. IC 32-31-5-6 says that unless a court orders otherwise, a landlord may not block access to or possession of the unit, and the section lists changing locks, adding a device that keeps the tenant out, and removing doors, windows, fixtures or appliances.

The same section also prohibits interrupting or shutting off electricity, gas, water or other essential services, with exceptions for emergencies, good-faith repairs and necessary construction. The statute does not apply when a unit is abandoned, which means the tenant failed to pay or offer to pay rent due and the circumstances would lead a reasonable person to conclude the unit was surrendered. A rental agreement cannot define abandonment differently.

Showing the house to buyers

Showings are allowed with limits. A tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for inspections, repairs, supplying services or showing the unit to buyers, lenders, prospective tenants, workers or contractors. In return the landlord must give reasonable notice, written or oral, enter at reasonable times, and avoid using the right of entry to harass the tenant. No notice is needed in an emergency that threatens occupants or the property, or when entry is under a court order.

A seller who schedules buyer visits through the listing agent should pass the same notice standard along, since a missed courtesy can turn into a dispute that delays closing.

What happens to the tenants and the rent when an Indiana landlord sells?

The sale is valid without the tenant's agreement. Indiana Code 32-31-1-10 says a landlord's conveyance is effective "without the attornment of the tenant," meaning the tenant does not have to accept the new owner for the transfer to count.

One rule protects tenants from confusion about who gets the rent. If a tenant pays rent to the original landlord before learning of the sale, that payment binds the new owner. Once the tenant has notice, the statute offers no such protection for later payments. Telling tenants in writing as soon as the sale closes, and naming the new payee, closes that gap.

The deposit has its own section, IC 32-31-3-19, titled "Sale of Property; Liability for Deposits; Exceptions." Chapter 3 also contains separate sections on return of deposits, notice of damages, remittance of the full deposit and liability for withheld deposits, so a seller should read the deposit chapter as a whole and keep a ledger for every tenant.

What disclosures does an Indiana landlord owe a tenant?

Indiana asks a landlord to put several things in writing, and some of them bind whoever buys the property next. A new owner who takes over a rental inherits the duty to keep these current.

  • Manager and agent. At or before the start of the rental agreement, the landlord, or a person who signs for the landlord, must give the tenant the name and address of an Indiana resident manager and an Indiana resident agent who is reasonably accessible and can accept legal papers and notices. One person can fill both roles. The duty binds any successor landlord, owner or manager (IC 32-31-3-18).
  • Flood plain. For agreements entered into or renewed after June 30, 2009, the landlord must say so in the rental agreement if the lowest floor, including any basement, is at or below the 100-year flood elevation (IC 32-31-1-21).
  • Military installation. A separate section covers disclosure of property near a military installation (IC 32-31-1-21.1).

A landlord who skips the manager and agent disclosure becomes the agent of each landlord for receiving legal process and notices, and the tenant can recover reasonable expenses spent finding the required names and addresses. The same chapter has sections on requests for law enforcement or emergency assistance and limits on penalties (IC 32-31-1-22), and on the death or incapacitation of a tenant (IC 32-31-1-23).

How should a landlord prepare a tenant-occupied Indiana house for sale?

Gather the paperwork first, then handle notices in the order the statutes expect. A clean file helps any buyer, including an investor who plans to keep the tenants.

  • Pull the signed lease, every renewal and any written changes to the rental agreement.
  • Confirm that the manager and agent disclosure was given and update it for the new owner.
  • Check the flood plain status and whether the lease says so where the statute requires.
  • Set showing dates with written notice and keep copies.
  • Decide whether tenants stay or leave, and count the notice periods in the table above if they will leave.
  • Write down each deposit, the date it was paid, and the tenant's mailing address.

Free help exists for tenants and sometimes for small landlords. Indiana Legal Help, indianalegalhelp.org, lets people search for legal aid by county or ZIP code. Indiana Legal Services listed an intake line of 1-844-243-8570, Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., on a 2022 fact sheet, and the state courts keep housing resources at in.gov/courts/housing. Check current hours before you call.

More questions about Indiana Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How much notice does an Indiana landlord give for unpaid rent?

At least ten days. The tenant can stop the termination by paying the rent in full before the notice period ends, unless the parties agreed otherwise. If the tenant does not pay, the landlord still has to file a court case to evict.

Can a landlord change the locks to get a tenant out in Indiana?

No. IC 32-31-5-6 bars a landlord from blocking a tenant's access or possession unless a court orders it, and lists changing locks and removing doors or appliances. The statute also bars shutting off essential services, except in emergencies or for good-faith repairs and necessary construction.

Does a tenant have to leave when an Indiana landlord sells the house?

Not just because of the sale. The conveyance is valid without the tenant's agreement under IC 32-31-1-10, but the lease and the notice rules still control when a tenancy ends. A tenant's rent paid before learning of the sale counts against the new owner.

Can an Indiana landlord enter the unit to show it to buyers?

Yes, with reasonable notice at reasonable times. The tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for showing the unit to buyers. An emergency allows entry without notice, and a landlord cannot use entry to harass a tenant.

Can a city in Indiana cap rent or add its own deposit rules?

Generally no. IC 32-31-1-20 voids local rules on rental rates, deposits, fees, lease terms and required disclosures unless a state statute authorizes them. Housing that receives government funds for reduced rents is an exception.

What is the small claims limit for rent and damages in Indiana?

Indiana Legal Help gives a small claims limit of $10,000 for the damages hearing in an eviction case.

Indiana probate law decides who inherits when there is no will, when a small estate can skip full probate, and who can sign a deed for an inherited house.

What the official sources say

  • Surviving spouse takes 1/2 of the net estate if the intestate leaves a child or issue of a deceased child; 3/4 if no issue but a parent survives; all if no issue or parent. (IC 29-1-2-1(b); source)
  • A childless second or subsequent spouse, where the decedent left children by a prior spouse, takes only 25% of the real property net value (but the same personal property share). (IC 29-1-2-1(c); source)
  • Small estate affidavit may be used 45 days after death if the gross probate estate (less liens, encumbrances, funeral expenses) does not exceed $100,000 for deaths after June 30, 2022 ($50,000 for deaths 2006 to mid-2022). (IC 29-1-8-1(a); source)
